editorNote: A movie phenomenon reaches the Commodore 64 while the home-computer counter weighs a new $300 machine against established game libraries.
morningLine: Ghostbusters heads for the C64; Commodore pitches an office in ROM, and local bulletin boards connect the neighborhood.

lead.headline: Ghostbusters Haunts the Commodore 64
lead.dek: Activision turns the summer film sensation into an October home-computer game, giving the game shelf this week’s biggest name.
body: Ghostbusters is crossing from the movie theater to the Commodore 64. Release listings place Activision’s North American C64 edition on Friday, October 26; a separate catalog confirms an October 1984 C64 release. The precise Friday date rests on the release listing rather than a contemporary day-of-sale advertisement, but the game plainly belongs on this October shelf.

The license has unusual recognition for a computer game. The film was still in domestic theaters during this weekend, appearing on the October 26–28 box-office chart, while its title now appears on a home-computer game. For C64 owners, that puts one of the year’s most recognizable screen names within reach of the disk drive.

This is a game-led week even as hardware makers court the same shoppers. Commodore is readying the Plus/4, a $300 machine with 64K and productivity software built in, yet the already-established Commodore 64 has the game catalog that makes a new film adaptation a retail event. The two products point to different answers to the same question: what will families actually do with a computer at home?

Exact store availability and a retail price for Ghostbusters are not established by the sources in hand. The release record supports the arrival of the C64 edition, while the broader October story is the competition for living-room attention among software, games and new hardware.

stories.headline: Commodore Puts a $300 Office in the Plus/4
body: Commodore’s Plus/4 is moving toward buyers with a different home-computer promise: productivity software built into the machine. An October COMPUTE! hands-on report describes a 64K computer priced at about $300, positioning it as a ready-made working tool rather than merely an empty platform awaiting programs.

That price places the Plus/4 squarely in the family-computer aisle, but the software-in-ROM approach is its sharper distinction. Buyers comparing machines this autumn will weigh the convenience of built-in applications against the deep third-party catalogs of established systems, including the C64 now receiving Ghostbusters.

The magazine’s account is an October rollout report, not evidence of a fresh October 22 announcement. It does, however, show Commodore trying to broaden the household computer pitch from play and programming to everyday office tasks.

stories.headline: The Neighborhood Bulletin Board Takes Shape
body: A modem and a local phone call can turn a home computer into a gathering place. Kathy Yakal’s period reporting for COMPUTE! describes boards run by enthusiasts, offering messages, public-domain files, games and communities built around particular machines. Chicago sysop John Semenek recalled finding one local board roughly two years earlier and at least 20 by the reporting period.

Stan and Susie Subeck’s Atari-oriented Valley Girl BBS gives the culture a playful face, with themed menus and online adventure games and trivia. This is not a national network in miniature so much as a collection of local rooms, each shaped by its operator and callers.

Keeping a board alive is no small hobby expense. A survey cited in the article put typical startup costs above $3,000 and continuing costs near $50 a month, before counting the sysop’s time. The November issue dating makes this period context, not a claim that these boards began operating this week.

stories.headline: BYTE Measures the IBM PC/AT’s 6 MHz Pace
body: The IBM PC/AT remains a prominent subject for the business-computer press. BYTE’s October coverage examines the machine and its 6 MHz Intel 80286 processor, a step in the IBM-compatible performance race.

The PC/AT was introduced in August, so this is a contemporary magazine assessment rather than a new October launch. Its presence beside inexpensive home machines shows how wide the computer market has become: a family comparing software shelves and an office comparing processor power are reading very different specifications.

curiosity.headline: On this BBS, deleting a message means to “bag” it
curiosity.summary: A Chicago-area Atari bulletin board styled its commands in Valley Girl slang.
curiosity.detail: The Subecks’ Valley Girl BBS called exiting “de-val”; its 13-year-old co-helper inspired the theme, according to Kathy Yakal.
